extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of Last Week Tonight, and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview
extracted.subtask_description: Producing and broadcasting long-form satirical segments on a televised late-night/comedy-news program, including editorial, legal, and distribution considerations. Covers how content choices (targeting public figures, mockery, stunts) interact with platform policies, legal risk, and audience/reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guinness World Records participation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Guinness refused [to send an adjudicator] stating that because their brand was 'aligned with kids and families', they would not send an adjudicator; it was their policy 'not to partake in any activities which may belittle their achievements or subject them to ridicule'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to stunts that mock existing record holders: Guinness may decline involvement if a record-attempt appears intended to ridicule a person or group; brand positioning (e.g., family-friendly) informs decisions. The page also reports Oliver's allegation that Guinness offered to certify after the fact only if he signed an agreement not to criticize their practices — an example of post-hoc certification conditioned on contractual restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal vetting and defamation/SLAPP risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments criticizing individuals or organizations carry defamation risk; HBO believed Last Week Tonight had done nothing wrong and described some suits as 'frivolous.' Despite vetting, Oliver acknowledged content could still lead to lawsuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should legally vet segments that allege wrongdoing or use potentially defamatory material; expect possible litigation costs (the Murray case reportedly cost HBO $200,000 and tripled the show's libel insurance fees). Even well-vetted satire can provoke SLAPP or defamation suits, so maintain libel insurance and be prepared for reputational/legal defense. Consulting First Amendment and defamation experts is recommended; legal opinions may vary on specific stunts (e.g., offers to public officials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate distribution/censorship constraints from regional/rightsholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional streaming rights-holders may refuse to carry politically sensitive or mocking content: Disney+ Hotstar refused to stream an episode satirizing Narendra Modi, and Hotstar reportedly began to censor jokes regarding Disney characters (example: the claim Donald Duck had a corkscrew penis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing material that targets political figures, state institutions, or a media company's own IP/characters, anticipate that international or corporate distribution partners may geo-block, refuse to stream, or require edits. Plan distribution strategies (alternate platforms, edits, or contextualization) and be aware of how acquisitions (e.g., by larger corporations) can change censorship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for verifiability / sourcing in public-facing summarizations
rubrics_metrics.description: This section [of the article] 'needs additional citations for verification. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For encyclopedia-style or public summaries of comedic/political interventions, ensure claims about controversies, legal outcomes, payments, or impacts are supported by reliable sources. Unsourced or poorly sourced claims (especially about legal matters or individuals) are vulnerable to challenge and removal; maintain transparent sourcing when documenting stunts, donations, or legal disputes.
